blocks.content: The last six topics covered inner join, left join, right join, full join, self join, and cross join, one at a time. An actual interview question rarely names the join type directly, it describes a real requirement and expects you to recognize which join type answers it.

This closing topic pulls all six join types together into the kind of question actually asked in interviews, recognizing the right join type from the wording alone, plus two genuinely common worked patterns, finding rows with no match and detecting duplicates.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364394749-155487112.png
blocks.alt: Interview questions rarely name a join type directly; the real skill is recognizing which join a question needs

blocks.content: 1. The Question Behind Every Join Interview Question
blocks.text: 1. The Question Behind Every Join Interview Question

blocks.content: Almost every join interview question is genuinely a disguised version of one of the six join types already covered. Find customers with no orders is a left join in disguise. Find employees who share a manager is a self join in disguise.
Recognizing the disguise matters more than remembering join syntax, since the syntax itself is genuinely the easy part once the right join type has actually been identified.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364394749-155487112.png
blocks.alt: Recognizing which join type a question describes matters more than remembering join syntax itself

blocks.content: 2. Spotting Which Join Type a Question Actually Needs
blocks.text: 2. Spotting Which Join Type a Question Actually Needs

blocks.content: A few real phrases map directly onto specific join types. Only rows that genuinely match on both sides points at an inner join. Every row from one specific table, matched or not, points at a left or right join. Rows with no match at all on one side points at a left or right join combined with an IS NULL filter.
Reading the question for these signals first, before writing a single line of SQL, genuinely saves time and avoids reaching for the wrong join type entirely.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364396695-998645674.png
blocks.alt: Specific phrases in a question map onto specific join types, before any SQL gets written at all

3. A Worked Example: Customers With No Orders
blocks.text: 3. A Worked Example: Customers With No Orders

blocks.content: This is genuinely one of the most common join interview questions asked. Find every customer who has never placed an order needs every customer row kept, matched or not, then filtered down to only the ones with no genuine match at all.

SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
blocks.code:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

codes.sql:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

blocks.content: The left join keeps every customer. The WHERE clause then isolates exactly the customers where no genuine order row was found, which is precisely what the question actually asked for.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364398668-371653739.png
blocks.alt: A left join combined with an IS NULL filter finds customers with genuinely zero orders

blocks.content: 4. A Worked Example: Detecting Duplicate Rows
blocks.text: 4. A Worked Example: Detecting Duplicate Rows

blocks.content: Find users who genuinely share the same email address is a classic self join question. A self join comparing every row against every other row on the email column, with an id comparison to avoid pairing a row with itself, surfaces exactly the duplicates.

SELECT u1.id, u2.id
FROM users u1
JOIN users u2 ON u1.email=u2.email
AND u1.id<u2.id;
blocks.code:
SELECT u1.id, u2.id
FROM users u1
JOIN users u2 ON u1.email=u2.email
AND u1.id<u2.id;

codes.sql:
SELECT u1.id, u2.id
FROM users u1
JOIN users u2 ON u1.email=u2.email
AND u1.id<u2.id;

blocks.content: Each row in this result represents a genuinely duplicate pair, two different user ids sharing the exact same email address, without the same pair appearing twice in reverse order.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364400198-516385811.png
blocks.alt: A self join with an id comparison finds pairs of rows sharing a genuinely duplicate email address

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: This exact pattern, self join plus an id comparison, is genuinely the standard interview answer for any find duplicate rows question, not just duplicate emails specifically.
5. A Worked Example: Generating Every Combination
blocks.text: 5. A Worked Example: Generating Every Combination

blocks.content: Generate every possible pairing between two lists, with no filtering condition at all, is genuinely a cross join question, even when the question never says the words cross join directly.

The signal here is the total absence of any real matching condition. If the question genuinely wants everything paired with everything, a cross join is the only join type that produces that result correctly.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364402232-515173119.png
blocks.alt: A question asking for every possible pairing with no filtering condition is genuinely a cross join in disguise

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: If you find yourself trying to write an ON clause for a question that has no real matching condition at all, that is genuinely a sign the question actually needs a cross join instead.
6. Genuinely Common Mistakes

A few real patterns undermine join interview answers specifically. Writing SQL immediately instead of first identifying which join type the question actually needs. Confusing a find rows with no match question with a plain inner join, which would return nothing at all instead of the unmatched rows actually wanted.
And forgetting the id comparison on a self join question, producing self pairs and reversed duplicates instead of the clean duplicate pairs actually expected.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364403848-189031388.png
blocks.alt: Common interview mistakes: writing SQL too early, confusing an anti join with inner join, and forgetting the self join id comparison
